newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemalan farmers reject guerrilla resettlement.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalan farmers reject guerrilla resettlement.

text.p: Government negotiators were working on Tuesday to calm tensions in a northern Guatemalan town where farmers, resentful after 36 years of war, rejected the resettlement of a group of ex-guerrillas, officials said.

Residents of Pueblo Nuevo, a farming cooperative near the Mexican border in the province of Quiche, over the weekend violently rejected 30 ex-combatants from the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) who hoped to settle there.

Some 300 peasants threatened to burn down houses built for the former URNG fighters and then cut off their exit when the ex-guerrillas tried to leave. Police confirmed that locals attempted to lynch two ex-guerrillas.

"Government representatives and the community are negotiating to seek a solution," Carlos Urrutia, spokesman for the U.N. Mission for Human Rights Verification in Guatemala (MINUGUA), told Reuters on Tuesday.

The violence and ensuing standoff mark the first hitch in the resettlement of guerrillas under terms of a Dec. 29 peace agreement between the government and the URNG, ending Central America's last and longest civil war.

Members of the Pueblo Nuevo cooperative will decide on Thursday whether to allow the guerrilla resettlement, Raquel Zelaya of the Government Peace Secretariat, which oversees compliance with peace accords, told reporters on Tuesday.

More than 3,000 members of the URNG are returning this week to their communities or looking for new areas to settle after living for three months in temporary disarmament camps where they turned in weapons.

The department of Quiche, populated mostly by Indians, was scarred by massacres of peasants and the burning of entire villages during the early 1980s when army counter-insurgency campaigns aimed to wipe out civilian support for guerrillas.

Many rural communities felt trapped between the army and the URNG and are now reluctant to accept former combatants from either side. The Pueblo Nuevo farming cooperative is community with an especially delicate balance because it includes former internal refugees.
